snippet.textDisplay: I was the caregiver for both my parents and inlaws. I never took any hostility from them personally. I knew they were frustrated, frightened and overwhelmed at times. I was truly their safe target. They knew deep down I wasn’t going away and would do my best for them. I never told them after the episode what happened because it would only make them sad. Just like if they ask for the 100th time ‘what time is it?’, I just tell them the time. Telling them only makes them feel bad, just answer the question as if for the first time because, for them, it is the first time. Feeling that connection was such a blessing. It is exhausting but so worth it.

One of the best pieces of advice I was given by the Dementia hotline was after one of the worst arguments ever, I was a mess. Thank-you for explaining why we see and feel the worst of the behaviour. 🙏🇦🇺💕

snippet.textDisplay:
YES! Spot on. This is also true of toddlers and teenagers learning about the world, and their own selves. Same with elders in transition. The acting out is usually a struggle for control.
When elders lose control of their physical body; their eyesight is not as good; their sense of smell is gone; they can’t do physical things they used to be able to do. Their social life diminishes. These things are unfamiliar, frustrating, and scary. It’s good to acknowledge the situation and the feelings that go with it.

snippet.textDisplay: I took care of my mom at the end.  My mom was an incredibly strong vibrant woman who took on the world and won.  She would not show fear at all. I just smiled and felt so good that she felt comfortable around me.   Although they put her on some heavy steroids due to brain cancer.  The doctor warned me she would say the most vile, disgusting things, and she would have no control over it.  It's a side effect of the medication.  Holy fuk was the doctor right.  She said things that could melt a marble statue.

While don’t need to be anyones ‘favorite’…it would’ve been nice if, for once I might’ve had the experience of being shown an ounce of reciprocal care, concern or compassion with respect for having worked tirelessly to stay present for them if not, be in a place where’d continue to predictably, ‘be there’ for theirs if/when they suffered and sought comfort of unconditional love, kindness and acceptance.

snippet.textDisplay: My father in law has been antagonistic and high conflict his whole life.  Now he demands his five sons come to constant meetings with the Dr, the nursing home, the lawyer. He complains bitterly that his daughters-in-law and grandchildren have terribly neglected his wife, who he uses to demand filial duty above and beyond. He forgets all we’ve done and appreciates nothing. Professionals recognize this as a pattern but the sons are critical of their wives and adult children because of their father’s complaints. It’s fraying every marriage. He will leave a terrible legacy. The sons are victims of childhood trauma from him. They can’t see the injustice. I’ve spent 40 years helping my husband survive being his father’s son.
